newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Upbeat economic data mask policy gloom in Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: Upbeat economic data mask policy gloom in Vietnam.

text.p: Vietnam issued figures on Tuesday showing continued signs of a healthy economy despite deepening political concern over trade problems, corruption, inflation and a range of other woes.
Data issued by the State Statistics Office showed industrial output up 13.5 percent between January and October compared with the same period last year.
There was also positive news on trade. The deficit fell slightly, for the first time in months, to $3.35 billion from a record level of $3.54 billion just one month earlier.
Exports from the beginning of the year until October 15 were put at $5.53 billion and imports at $8.88 billion.
Just days ago, inflation figures were announced showing a year-on-year price rise of 2.9 percent, down from double digit levels in 1995 and triple digit levels only a few years earlier.
But Tuesday's otherwise positive news came amid a climate of pessimism in Hanoi and signs of differences within the government over management of the socialist country's previously gleaming economy.
In a weekend interview with Reuters, former Foreign Minister Nguyen Co Thach spoke of forces that were calling for import substitution and opposing principles of free trade.
Two weeks earlier, Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet launched the current session of Vietnam's National Assembly with an uncharacteristic downbeat assessment of the economic outlook.
In a lengthy speech to assembled delegates, diplomats and journalists he painted a picture of stagnation, listing woes from corruption and vice to revenue problems and trade.
"I think what you're seeing is a slowdown that's arising out of the fear of capitalism," said a senior Vietnamese economist.

"The government is worried whether they should turn left or turn right. There is no turning left. But to turn right towards capitalism is to turn towards something they've been fighting against for years."

Western analysts say Vietnam's economy remains on track, despite worries over the trade gap and a current account deficit that has been put at an unsustainably high 15 percent of gross domestic product.
But they also point to emerging differences of opinion in Hanoi over the management of market reform policies introduced in the late 1980s in place of a Soviet-style command-led system.

In a sign of the prevailing mood, Tuesday's English-language Vietnam News carried a front-page story criticising the thinking behind a drive for economic growth that had left farmers unprotected from the price fluctuations of a market economy.
"They have been very poor because of the country's backward economy and are now being left behind while the whole population's living standard has improved," the report said.
Around 80 percent of Vietnam's 75 million population derives a living from farming.
